title: Lecture 2 · Dijkstra's algorithm
summary: Relaxation on the board, a full trace of the running example, why settled distances stay fixed, and a negative-edge counterexample.

notes.title: A cheaper route lowers a tentative distance
notes.context: On the board the edge from \(S\) gives \(B\) the tentative distance \(6\).
notes.text: Later the path through \(C\) offers \(4 + 1 = 5\), so relaxation lowers \(d(B)\) to \(5\) and makes \(C\) its parent.

highlights.title: Tracing Dijkstra on the running example
highlights.teaches: Each step settles the smallest tentative distance and relaxes its edges, ending with \(d(G) = 8\).
points: The settled order is \(S, E, A, C, B, D, G\).
Two relaxations improve a value: \(B\) from \(6\) to \(5\), \(G\) from \(9\) to \(8\).

steps.action: Write \(S = 0\) and every other vertex at \(\infty\).
steps.why: Only the source has a known distance.

steps.action: Settle \(S\), \(E\) and \(A\) in order of distance.
steps.why: \(0 < 1 < 2\): each is the smallest open value when it is chosen.

highlights.title: Why a settled distance never changes
highlights.teaches: With non-negative weights, no path that leaves the settled set can undercut the smallest tentative distance.
points: Any other path to the chosen vertex leaves the settled set first.
Non-negative edges after that point can only add cost.

highlights.title: A negative edge breaks the settled order
highlights.teaches: With \(w(Y, X) = -2\), \(X\) is settled at \(2\) although the path through \(Y\) costs \(1\).
points: \(X\) has the smaller tentative distance, so it is settled first.
